terms.formal: Deep-lung breath analysis mechanism - the ignition interlock, CCP Arts. 17.441 and 42A.408
terms.short: Breathalyzer wired to your car's ignition. Statute's actual words.
terms.long: It sounds invented, but "deep-lung breath analysis mechanism" is the statute's own phrase for an ignition interlock - a breath tester wired to the car so it will not start if alcohol is detected. It is mandatory for repeat and aggravated intoxication offences.
terms.notes: CCP Art. 17.441(a) (bond) and Art. 42A.408(a) (community supervision) both use 'deep-lung breath analysis mechanism' verbatim. On probation it must stay installed not less than 50 percent of the supervision period. DISTINCTIVELY TEXAN PHRASING - elsewhere it is just called an IID or interlock, so the phrase will sound bizarre to non-Texans and is worth a card for that reason alone.

terms.formal: Battering Intervention and Prevention Program, CCP Art. 42A.504(c)(1); programme established under CCP Art. 42.141 and accredited by TDCJ-CJAD
terms.short: Court-ordered classes for domestic violence offenders. Not anger management.
terms.long: BIPP is an accredited battering intervention and prevention programme a judge can order as a condition of community supervision in a family violence case. It is specifically not anger management and not general counselling, and the defendant must start within 60 days.
terms.notes: CCP Art. 42A.504(c)(1) authorises it; the programme itself is established by CCP Art. 42.141 and accredited by TDCJ's Community Justice Assistance Division with the Texas Council on Family Violence. Must be provided free if the defendant cannot pay (42A.504(d)). Judges usually announce it alongside the mandatory $100 payment to a family violence centre (42A.504(b)). Said as a word, rhyming with 'flip'. TEXAS-SPECIFIC ACRONYM - and it surprises people that the prison system accredits the classes. It is NOT in the Health and Safety Code.

terms.formal: Magistrate's Order for Emergency Protection, CCP Art. 17.292
terms.short: Emergency no-contact order issued at your first court appearance.
terms.long: A MOEP is an emergency protective order a magistrate issues at the first appearance after a family violence, assault, stalking or trafficking arrest. It is mandatory where there was serious bodily injury or a deadly weapon, and the alleged victim does not need to be present or to ask for it.
terms.notes: Said aloud as 'mope'. CCP Art. 17.292. Duration 61-91 days, or 91-121 days in a deadly weapon or serious bodily injury case; it also suspends any handgun licence. THREE DIFFERENT ORDERS GET CALLED 'PROTECTIVE ORDER' AND JUDGES USE THE PHRASE LOOSELY FOR ALL THREE: (1) the MOEP under Art. 17.292; (2) a CCP Chapter 7B order for sexual assault, trafficking or stalking - NOTE this was Chapter 7A until it was renumbered effective January 1, 2021, so older references and forms say 7A; (3) a Family Code Title 4 family violence protective order, two years by default. Violating one is a separate crime under Penal Code 25.07.

terms.formal: Outcry witness, CCP Art. 38.072
terms.short: First adult a child told about the abuse.
terms.long: In a child abuse case the first adult the child told about the abuse may repeat in court what the child said, even though that is normally inadmissible hearsay. The State must give 14 days' notice and the judge holds a reliability hearing outside the jury's presence first.
terms.notes: CCP Art. 38.072 - applies to a child under 18 or a person with a disability, and the outcry witness must be an adult other than the defendant. TEXAS-SPECIFIC: this is a named Texas hearsay exception and 'outcry' is Texas terminology. Related provisions on child testimony at Arts. 38.071 and 38.074. Only relevant in child sexual and physical abuse prosecutions, but central when it is.

terms.formal: Penitentiary packet - certified TDCJ records offered to prove prior convictions
terms.short: Certified prison records proving your prior convictions.
terms.long: A pen packet is a certified bundle of TDCJ records - judgment, photograph, fingerprints - offered during the punishment phase to prove that the defendant is the same person named in those older convictions. It comes in without a records custodian because the statute makes it self-authenticating.
terms.notes: CCP Art. 42.09 Sec. 8(b-1): 'A document certified under Subsection (b) is self-authenticated for the purposes of Rules 901 and 902, Texas Rules of Evidence' - that is why no witness from Huntsville is needed. The phrase 'pen packet' is practitioner usage, not statutory, but it is thoroughly entrenched in Texas appellate opinions including San Antonio's Fourth Court. Bexar's District Clerk separately prepares 'penitentiary packets to be sent with the defendant to the prison upon conviction'.

terms.formal: The Michael Morton Act, CCP Art. 39.14 - Texas's criminal discovery statute
terms.short: Texas open-file law. Prosecutors must hand over their evidence.
terms.long: The Michael Morton Act is Texas's open-file discovery law, named after a man who served nearly 25 years because a prosecutor withheld evidence. Lawyers usually just say "39.14". Its disclosure duty for favourable evidence is broader than the federal Brady rule.
terms.notes: CCP Art. 39.14; enacted as S.B. 1611, 83rd Leg. (2013), indexed by the Legislature under the subject 'MICHAEL MORTON ACT'. Art. 39.14(h) codifies the Brady duty in broader terms: the State 'shall disclose ... any exculpatory, impeachment, or mitigating document, item, or information' - with no materiality threshold and no need for the defence to request it. I did not separately fetch Brady v. Maryland, so present the comparison as read off the Texas text.

terms.formal: Motion to set aside, or exception to, an indictment or information - CCP Art. 27.02(1)
terms.short: Attack on the indictment itself, not the evidence.
terms.long: A motion to quash attacks the charging document rather than the evidence - arguing the indictment fails to allege an offence, is barred by limitations, or is defective in form. Practically, if it succeeds the State usually just re-indicts.
terms.notes: NAMING: the Code never uses the word 'quash'. CCP Art. 27.02(1) calls it 'A motion to set aside or an exception to an indictment or information for some matter of form or substance'. Grounds are enumerated at Art. 27.08 (substance) and Art. 27.09 (form, including that it was 'not returned by a lawfully chosen or empaneled grand jury'). TIMING TRAP: Art. 1.14(b) - failing to object before trial waives and forfeits the objection, and it cannot be raised on appeal. Carry both names in any on-screen card.
also_said: motion to set aside the indictment

terms.formal: Allocution before sentencing, CCP Art. 42.07 - the question whether the defendant has anything to say why sentence should not be pronounced
terms.short: Ritual question before sentencing. Only three answers count legally.
terms.long: Just before pronouncing sentence the judge asks whether there is any legal reason the sentence should not be pronounced. It sounds like an invitation to speak, but Texas law recognises only three valid answers: the defendant has been pardoned, he is presently incompetent, or he is not the person convicted. Defence counsel almost always answers "no legal reason".
terms.notes: CCP Art. 42.07. THIS IS NOT THE FEDERAL ALLOCUTION RIGHT - Fed. R. Crim. P. 32(i)(4) gives a genuine right to address the court in mitigation, whereas Art. 42.07 is a narrow legal challenge. I did not separately fetch the federal rule, so state the contrast carefully. Related: Art. 42.03 Sec. 1(a) requires sentence be pronounced in the defendant's presence, and Sec. 1(b) puts the victim impact statement strictly AFTER sentencing, with the court reporter forbidden to transcribe it - which is why victim statements are missing from transcripts.
also_said: legal reason why sentence should not be pronounced

terms.formal: Charge of the court - the written jury instructions, CCP Arts. 36.14-36.16
terms.short: Texas's name for the written jury instructions.
terms.long: Texas says "the charge of the court" where most places say "jury instructions". It is a physical document of the law the jury must apply, and in Texas the judge delivers it BEFORE closing arguments, so the lawyers argue against the instructions the jury has already received.
terms.notes: CCP Art. 36.14 requires the written charge be delivered before argument begins - the reverse of federal practice, where instructions usually follow argument. The charge goes to the jury room. Bexar County's own juror information page uses the capitalised phrase: 'After the Charge of the Court, the lawyers have the opportunity to summarize the evidence in their closing arguments.' TEXAS DIFFERENCE CONFIRMED IN BOTH THE NAME AND THE ORDERING.

terms.formal: Publication of admitted exhibits to the jury; see CCP Art. 36.25
terms.short: Actually showing admitted evidence to the jury.
terms.long: "Published" has nothing to do with publishing. Evidence goes through four steps that sound like one: marked (labelled), offered (formally tendered), admitted (the judge says yes - only now is it evidence), and published (actually shown, read or played to the jury).
terms.notes: CCP Art. 36.25: 'There shall be furnished to the jury upon its request any exhibits admitted as evidence.' The four-step sequence is the most frequently spoken exchange in any trial and 'published' is the word that most reliably confuses lay viewers. No Texas-vs-other-states difference - this entry earns its place purely on confusion value.

terms.formal: Courthouse slang for a parole pre-revocation warrant issued under Government Code Sec. 508.251
terms.short: Parole violation hold. Usually no bond, so no release.
terms.long: A blue warrant is a hold placed on someone accused of violating parole. No judge issues it - the parole division does - and it usually carries no bond, so a defendant can make bail on the new criminal charge and still not walk out of the jail.
terms.notes: SLANG ONLY - FLAGGED. The phrase 'blue warrant' appears nowhere on TDCJ's site or in statute; TDCJ's own term is 'pre-revocation warrant'. Every source using 'blue warrant' was a defence or bail-bond blog, which I did not rely on. Present it as courthouse slang for a pre-revocation warrant under Gov't Code Sec. 508.251, and do NOT attribute the phrase to TDCJ or to a statute. The mechanism is certain and appears constantly; the wording is what is uncertain.

terms.formal: Expunction of criminal records, CCP Chapter 55A
terms.short: Erases the record entirely. Only if never convicted.
terms.long: An expunction destroys the records of an arrest and case. It is generally available only to people who were not convicted - acquitted, dismissed, or no-billed. It is the stronger of the two Texas record remedies.
terms.notes: CHAPTER NUMBER CHANGED - CITE 55A, NOT 55. Expunction was recodified into CCP Chapter 55A by Acts 2023, 88th Leg., Ch. 765 (H.B. 4504), effective January 1, 2025; CR.55 now returns a 404. ONE-LINER FOR SCREEN: expunction erases, nondisclosure hides. Successful deferred adjudication generally gets nondisclosure, not expunction.

terms.formal: Order of nondisclosure of criminal history record information, Government Code Chapter 411, Subchapter E-1
terms.short: Seals the record from employers. Police still see it.
terms.long: An order of nondisclosure seals a record rather than destroying it. The public and most employers cannot see it, but law enforcement, prosecutors and licensing agencies still can. This is the usual remedy after successfully completing deferred adjudication.
terms.notes: Gov't Code Ch. 411, Subch. E-1. CCP Art. 42A.111(e) requires the judge discharging a deferred adjudication either to grant nondisclosure or to tell the defendant when he becomes eligible. Drug court graduates get one by statute, but never on a DWI (Gov't Code 123.001(c)). Contrast with expunction, which destroys the record - and note that deferred adjudication is NOT an expunction, which is the most common viewer misconception about it.

terms.formal: Bail pending appeal, CCP Art. 44.04(b)
terms.short: No bail while appealing if sentence is ten years or more.
terms.long: A defendant who is convicted and appeals cannot be released on bond if the punishment is ten years or more, or if the offence is on the 42A.054 list - the statute says he shall immediately be placed in custody. This is why someone can be taken away in handcuffs on the spot even though the case is going up on appeal.
terms.notes: CCP Art. 44.04(b), which uses the phrase 'shall immediately be placed in custody'. Explains an on-camera moment that otherwise looks arbitrary. Related: a motion for new trial must be filed within 30 days of sentencing in open court (not of the verdict), and is overruled by operation of law if the judge does not rule within 75 days - Texas Rules of Appellate Procedure 21.4 and 21.8.

terms.formal: Sex offender registration program, CCP Chapter 62
terms.short: Required registry. Deferred adjudication still triggers it.
terms.long: Registration duties run for ten years after discharge or release for most reportable offences, and for life for a sexually violent offence. Critically, deferred adjudication counts - there is no conviction, but the duty to register still attaches.
terms.notes: CCP Art. 62.101(a) (duty ends when the person dies, for a sexually violent offence) and 62.101(c) (ten years from the later of discharge or release). Art. 62.001(5) defines 'reportable conviction or adjudication' to INCLUDE deferred adjudication - the single most misunderstood point for viewers, and it must be admonished at the plea under CCP Art. 26.13(a)(5). Judges commonly pair it with the child safety zone, no going within 1,000 feet of premises where children commonly gather (Art. 42A.453(c)), sex offender treatment (42A.452) and a DNA sample (42A.451).

terms.formal: Jury shuffle - reshuffling of the jury panel, CCP Art. 35.11
terms.short: Either side can demand the jury panel be reshuffled.
terms.long: Either side may demand once, without giving any reason, that the entire jury panel's seating order be randomly reshuffled. It matters because lawyers strike jurors in seating order, so the shuffle can move who is likely to end up on the jury.
terms.notes: MECHANISM STATUTORY, WORD IS NOT. CCP Art. 35.11 provides the reshuffling right, but the word 'shuffle' appears nowhere in the statute - it is slang left over from the pre-1991 practice of physically shuffling juror name cards, and it is judicially entrenched in dozens of appellate opinions. A DISTINCTLY TEXAN ODDITY worth explaining to outsiders. Related: ten peremptory strikes per side in a non-capital felony (Art. 35.15(b)), and Texas codified Batson at Art. 35.261 with an unusual remedy - the court 'shall call a new array' rather than merely reseating the juror. 'Venire' is real practitioner usage but the statute says 'general panel' and 'array'. I did not verify how often shuffles actually happen.
